item.title: What to Know About the Binance Hack
item.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that hackers had stolen some $6 billion in digital coins in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history.

The company said that it had halted withdrawals in response and that customers would get lost money back. While much about the hack is still unknown, details of how it happened and who might be responsible are beginning to come into focus.

Here’s what to know about the incident.

Binance is a marketplace for digital coins where customers can buy Bitcoin, Ether and other types of cryptocurrency. The platform was created in 2017. As of this summer, it had more than 320 million users, according to the company.

Like many crypto exchanges, Binance also allows customers to store their holdings with the expectation that it will keep their funds safe.

Three of the five biggest breaches have been carried out by North Korea, according to TRM Labs, an industry research firm.

Source: TRM Labs.

Aaron Krolik/The New York Times

Much of Binance’s success was built on offering risky services, like allowing investors to borrow money to place bets on the price of cryptocurrencies. It also drew in customers by allowing them to trade anonymously, and for several years did not collect basic information that traditional companies require to deter financial crime.

Binance has also weathered years of legal and regulatory problems. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to violating anti-money-laundering laws and paid $4.3 billion in penalties to the U.S. government. The company’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, was sentenced to four months in federal prison. After completing his sentence, he moved to the United Arab Emirates.

In October 2025, Mr. Zhao was pardoned by President Trump. Binance has a business relationship with the Trump family crypto business, World Liberty Financial, a major source of the president’s wealth.

Chainalysis and another analytics firm, TRM Labs, attributed the attack to an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. On Saturday, the F.B.I. confirmed those findings.

TRM Labs said that the hack began on Thursday at around 4 p.m. Eastern time, when an attacker moved more than $6 billion out of Binance wallets, most of it in just about 20 minutes. A second wave occurred around two hours later.

Binance initially said that the hackers might have compromised an engineer’s laptop, leading to unauthorized withdrawals. But in an update on social media on Friday, the company said that had identified “additional points of breach.” It did not provide more details.

Binance said it was working with law enforcement. TRM Labs said TraderTraitor was also behind a February 2025 hack of Bybit, another crypto exchange. In that attack, Bybit lost $1.5 billion, which at the time was the largest ever crypto heist.

Binance said that it would cover any customer losses using its company funds, which it had already set aside. It also said in a statement Friday that it had already begun “recovering affected assets for users,” without providing more detail.

Binance said that it had worked with partners in the industry to freeze around $3 billion in funds affected by the hack to prevent the hackers from selling them off. Tether, a major crypto platform, said it had frozen more than $1.5 billion in crypto, while Circle, another firm, said it had frozen more than $800 million.

The hack affected the original Binance (Binance.com), which the company blocks U.S. customers from using (though some probably do so anyway via virtual private networks). There is also a small Binance.Us platform for U.S. users in certain states, which was not part of the hack.

Binance plays a crucial role in the crypto industry, and news of the hack may affect confidence in cryptocurrencies and the exchanges where they are traded.

The price of Bitcoin, the largest cryptocurrency, dropped several percentage points, to below $80,000. Its value, however, remained well above lows over the summer, when Bitcoin traded for as little as $59,000.

item.title: The New Hot Job in Law Doesn’t Require a J.D.
item.description:
In 2018, when Daniel Himmel first moved from practicing law to a job that today might be called legal engineering, it felt like a big career risk.

“I was nervous,” he said. “I thought, what is my career going to look like? Where do I go from here?”

He doesn’t feel that way anymore. As the head of legal engineering for North America at the legal tech company Legora, Himmel has hired about 70 people over the past year. They’re part of a global team of about 200 legal engineers the company has built since 2024. “We’re hiring hundreds, and competitors are hiring them, and our clients are hiring them,” he said. “It’s a true profession.”

And it’s one of the hottest jobs in the rapidly changing world of law. As artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of legal work, technology vendors like Legora, law firms, and in-house legal teams are all looking for people who understand both law and technology well enough to rewrite work flows and teach others how to use A.I. tools.

Often, they’re called “legal engineers.” But they are also sometimes described as “knowledge and innovation counsels,” “innovation attorneys,” or “legal applications engineers.”

Exactly what the job entails varies from company to company, as does the salary: The law firm Latham & Watkins is hiring “legal engineering attorneys” in at least five cities, with a salary range of $220,000 to $250,000. An “A.I. innovation adviser” at Kirkland & Ellis can make between $153,000 and $220,000 a year, according to the company’s job listing, while Gibson Dunn is advertising a salary for a “legal technology & AI Attorney” between $250,000 to $300,000.

In-house legal teams have posted similar jobs. The chip maker Nvidia is hiring a “legal operations engineer” for $124,00 to $195,500 a year, and Microsoft wants a “principal legal engineer” at a salary between $147,000 and $278,900, according to job postings.

A.I. companies that make tools for law firms, including OpenAI, Thomson Reuters, and Google, are also hiring legal engineers.

Parameters of the job, which has expanded in both prevalence and scope in recent years, are still being defined. “If you were to just put it into an equation, it’s law plus technology plus business process,” said Irene Liu, the executive director of the A.I. initiative at Stanford Law School, which in September began promoting a two-week in-residence executive program called Legal Engineering Academy.

The program isn’t accepting applications yet, but about 1,400 senior leaders have signed up to be notified when it is — about half are part of in-house legal teams, and about 20 percent are law firm partners and senior attorneys, according to the school.

In the first six months of this year, almost 50 lawyers left the 200 largest law firms in the United States to move to A.I. companies, including 15 who moved into jobs with legal engineering titles, according to Firm Prospects, a platform for legal recruiters. (The collapse of the venerable law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges this week was another sign of the change sweeping through the industry.)

At A.I. companies, legal engineers sometimes help build tech for lawyers, but more typically help clients integrate the product into work flows, run trials and onboard employees. The legal A.I. giant Harvey has grown its team of legal engineers who do this type of work from 180 people to 215 people within the last two weeks (it advertises a salary range of $220,000 to $320,000 a year). All of them are former practicing lawyers.

Legal engineers employed by law firms often do similar work-flow design and educational work, but with a wider focus.

Ropes & Gray hired the first of its five legal engineers, whom it calls practice innovation attorneys, at the end of last year. “In the old days, there was technology and there was law. And as long as my email worked, I didn’t have to talk to people who dealt with the technology,” said Howard Glazer, a longtime partner at the firm who became its head of practice A.I. about a year ago. “But now we actually provide our service and provide our product using the tools.”

“‘Legal engineer’ kind of makes it sound like someone made it up,” he added. “But it’s not. It’s a role which the current environment just screams for.”

The law firm Latham & Watkins now has more than 100 people dedicated to its A.I. initiatives, it confirmed to DealBook. Some of them work on building proprietary technology, while others focus on A.I.-enabled work flows, encouraging lawyers to adopt them and other areas.

Virtually no schools offer formal training programs for legal engineers, though some have added classes. Many legal engineers are former practicing lawyers who taught themselves A.I. skills or learned on the job. Some have backgrounds in legal operations, paralegal work or consulting. Fewer are former software engineers who then went to law school — “the unicorn,” one hiring manager said.

Ankita Puri became a senior legal engineer at Legora after working in commercial litigation at a law firm, and then as the chief legal officer of a financial institution. She said she appreciates the greater diversity of work and more frequent interaction with clients that has come with the transition.

“It’s not so much going from actively practicing law to not,” she said. “I think it’s more embracing this generational shift in the legal industry.”

Mary O’Carroll, the C.E.O. of LegalEng Consulting Group, which works with in-house legal teams, has been an executive in legal operations for more than 20 years, including for 13 years at Google. She, too, sees the rise of legal engineers as part of a shift in the industry.

“You don’t necessarily need a giant pyramid of lawyers anymore,” she said. “People who have this kind of skill set don’t have to have a J.D., and they don’t have to be software engineers, but there’s business process re-engineering, or this M.B.A. type skill, that I think is really necessary.”

The position fits into what some see as a category of job becoming more essential in the A.I. era: Those that use specific expertise to design A.I. systems. LinkedIn job postings for “marketing engineer,” for example, increased 29 percent from 2024 to 2025 after relatively little growth in prior years, according to the company.

“What’s notable is that these titles are showing up well beyond traditional engineering. We are seeing them across functions like operations, product, business development, and even design,” Kory Kantenga, the head of economics at LinkedIn, said in a statement.

The lingering question is whether this type of job stays in hot demand. “It’s absolutely growing,” said Glazer of Ropes & Gray. “The question in my mind is going to be, you know, how long will it last? Is it a transition position?”

O’Carroll said she didn’t see the pace of change easing up, and that legal engineers will be needed to maintain systems and adapt to shifting technology and work.

Byong Kim, who became chief data & A.I. officer at the law firm Seyfarth Shaw last year after working in technology there for 13 years, said he thinks every law firm and every law department is looking to understand how to use A.I. more effectively right now.

“Long-term wise, I think we’re still trying to play out how this is all going to work out as technology gets better,” he said. “It’s still too early to say what the actual answer is, but I will say it’s a very interesting time for me. I don’t think I’ve ever been as busy.”

Binance suspended withdrawals after a massive hack. The crypto exchange said on Thursday that the hackers stole more than $6 billion in digital coins and that it would cover all losses. The attack appears to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist ever, and prominent crypto stocks and the price of Bitcoin slumped on Friday.

A prominent law firm plans to wind down. Weil, Gotshal & Manges has struggled amid an exodus of high-profile lawyers, a scuttled deal to merge with Willkie Farr & Gallagher, and a botched succession plan in which Ramona Nee, who had been expected to take over as the leader of the firm, turned down the top role. The firm said its senior leadership had recommended to dissolve the firm and would vote on the matter in the coming days.

Investors questioned the A.I. spending spree. The S&P 500 index fell more than 1 percent and the Nasdaq index fell more than 2 percent on Friday amid a bruising tech sell-off. Over the past two weeks, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta said they were on track to spend more than $720 billion this year on data centers and other capital expenses.

More big deals: Anthropic filed its S-1. DoorDash will buy Instacart for $17 billion. Kalshi landed a $40 billion valuation. And Kevin Warsh, the Federal Reserve’s chairman, said the central bank would alter its rate-setting meeting schedule next year.

It feels as if billionaires and Big Tech are on the ballot this election season. That’s especially true in California, where voters will decide on Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on the state’s ultrawealthy that supporters say is needed to offset federal health care budget cuts. Polling suggests the “billionaire tax” could go down in defeat on Tuesday.

The journalist Jonathan Weber has chronicled the rise of tech and its influence on politics, economics and culture for decades, including in his new book, “City on the Edge: Technology, Politics, and the Fight for the Soul of San Francisco.” He spoke with DealBook’s Bernhard Warner about the fight over the proposed tax, Big Tech money in politics, and the national significance of tech titans. The interview has been edited and condensed.

The Times recently reported that tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen, had become the biggest force in political giving, vastly outspending major donors Charles Koch and Ken Griffin. Did you see this coming?

The short answer is no. But it makes sense that the world’s largest industry — one with a lot at stake when it comes to regulation — would produce the biggest political donors.

Though how the money will be deployed is not as obvious. Once Trump is gone there’s likely to be a fracturing of the political right, and it’s unclear where people like Musk and Andreessen will come out on that.

There are still mainstream liberals in the industry, like investors Reid Hoffman and crypto mogul Chris Larsen. And, assuming there isn’t a big crash in the near future, we’re going to have a whole new generation of very young, very wealthy A.I. executives and investors whose political views are pretty unformed.

If Prop 40 fares well in California, similar measures could pop up across the country. What would its passage mean for California and the tech sector?

The main argument against the billionaire tax is that the wealthy would simply leave the state to avoid it, and thereby destroy Silicon Valley as we know it. Google’s Sergey Brin, who’s leading the charge against it, has already moved.

But I’m skeptical: Republicans have long argued that high taxes would drive businesses and wealthy people out of the state. While many companies have left, plenty have come in behind them. No other place has a tech ecosystem like California’s.

Brin and others are spending huge sums to defeat the tax. Can their money, influence and connections help defeat the ballot measure on Tuesday?

Opponents of the tax are pouring money into Prop 42, which would nullify the billionaire levy if it gets more votes. It’s telling that the tax’s opponents, including Governor Newsom, aren’t confident they can defeat it outright, even with a war chest of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s C.E.O., has gone a different route. He negotiated a deal with Meta’s board to create a new class of shares that ultimately will keep him in the state. What does that tell you about tech leaders’ response to this new tax threat?

I think this kind of maneuver will be more common than people actually moving to Texas or Florida.

Frankly, if the tax passes and people do start relocating, that’s likely to prompt more tax-the-rich efforts in the destination states.

item.title: How Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Went Down
item.description:
At about 4:20 p.m. on Thursday, a string of unusual transactions started to cause alarm at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Money was pouring out of the company’s accounts, a multibillion-dollar deluge of digital coins. It had all the hallmarks of a crypto heist — a high-speed bank robbery conducted over the internet.

As the news spread, Binance’s top executives put together an informal war room on Wea, the company’s internal messaging system, with about 100 participants, including specialized cryptocurrency tracers and security personnel.

They eventually transitioned to a mass conference call, with 100 boxes on the screen, where employees took turns muting and then unmuting, communicating in a mixture of English and Chinese. Among them was He Yi, Binance’s co-chief executive, who is seven months pregnant, and worked through the night from her base in Abu Dhabi, taking a call at 3 a.m. local time.

Ms. He and her colleagues were navigating one of the most damaging crises in Binance’s long and troubled history. A team of North Korean hackers had penetrated the exchange analysts said, and drained more than $6 billion in the largest crypto heist of all time. Binance was forced to halt deposits and withdrawals, and posted a series of frantic messages on X, promising that it would cover any losses.

It was a surreal situation made even more surreal by the actions of Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, who spent the evening narrating the events to his 12.9 million followers on X. He posted prayer hand emojis, publicly jousted with the site’s owner, Elon Musk, and insisted that “user funds are SAFU” — using a bit of crypto slang to reassure customers that hundreds of millions of dollars in deposits would not simply vanish into thin air.

“It hurts, but we will survive,” Mr. Zhao declared.

The impact of the Binance attack rippled across the crypto industry, from Abu Dhabi to New York, setting off a frantic effort to salvage some of the stolen funds and prompting law enforcement inquiries. This account of how the hack unfolded is based on interviews with four people with knowledge of the events, as well as analyses by crypto forensics firms and documents reviewed by The New York Times.

For years, Binance has been the most important and contentious company in the crypto world. After Mr. Zhao founded it in 2017, it quickly turned into a behemoth, the No. 1 destination for customers looking to convert traditional currencies into digital coins like Bitcoin and Ether.

It also became a haven for crime. In 2023, Binance pleaded guilty to anti-money-laundering violations that had allowed criminals to move money and paid $4.3 billion in penalties to U.S. regulators. Mr. Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison.

For all its troubles, however, Binance never lost popularity among the crypto faithful. It remains the world’s largest exchange by a distance, and Mr. Zhao, who lives in Abu Dhabi, is something of an industry folk hero. Binance’s main platform is banned in the United States. But last year, the company forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the Trump family crypto start-up. President Trump granted a pardon to Mr. Zhao last October, paving the way for Binance to expand into the U.S. market.

But on the night of Oct. 29, the company had to deal with the aftermath of the $6 billion hack.

Such attacks have become commonplace in the crypto world. In February 2025, the North Koreans stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, a rival exchange. Bybit was breached after Ben Zhou, its chief executive, approved a seemingly routine transaction that granted the thieves access to the exchange’s internal system.

It’s not clear precisely how the North Koreans got around Binance’s defenses. An initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop, Binance said Friday. But the company later said it had uncovered “additional points of breach.”

Much of the drama played out in public. Almost all crypto transactions are recorded on the blockchain, a ledger of money movements that anyone can look up. That meant crypto analysts could see funds leaving Binance in real time.

On Thursday afternoon, Jonathan Levin, the chief executive of the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, was on a video call with a former senior U.S. official, discussing the need for the U.S. government to deploy cyber attacks against adversaries. Then Mr. Levin got the news about Binance.

“I looked at my phone and was like, ‘Oh, this doesn’t look good,’” he said in an interview.

A group of Chainalysis employees gathered in a conference room in New York named “Silk Road,” after another crypto platform that was famously hacked. They worked until the early hours of Friday morning, eating Malaysian food and analyzing transactions to get a clearer picture of what had happened.

Soon both Chainalysis and another analytics firm, TRM Labs, attributed the attack to an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. North Koreans have targeted crypto companies for years, using the proceeds of those thefts to fund its nuclear program, according to Western officials.

The hackers have developed increasingly complex strategies to steal crypto and launder the proceeds, a painstaking endeavor that can take months to complete. In a blog post on Friday, Chainalysis said the attackers had deployed “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” conducting thousands of transactions over a short period, probably with the help of automation.

“The level of sophistication of these actors can’t be understated,” Mr. Levin said in the interview.

At the same time, Binance’s colleagues in the industry mobilized to intercept some of the laundered crypto. Certain digital coin issuers can freeze funds, allowing them to halt a money-laundering operation in its tracks.

Soon after the hack, Tether and Circle, two major issuers, announced that they had frozen stashes of their own coins that the hackers had seized from Binance, a combined total of more than $2 billion in crypto. Binance is now working to gain access to those funds, the company said.

But $2.4 billion in crypto is already “beyond any issuer’s reach,” according to TRM. In a social media post on Friday, Binance said that it had set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses from the hack.

How much money Binance has in reserve is not publicly known. After midnight, Mr. Musk posted a grimacing emoji underneath an X post comparing Mr. Zhao to Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced crypto mogul whose FTX exchange collapsed in 2022.

“Bad time to troll,” Mr. Zhao responded. “Please stop.” He noted that Binance owns over $1 billion in shares in SpaceX, Mr. Musk’s rocket company.

Mr. Zhao’s comment got the attention of Ms. He, Binance’s co-chief executive and his longtime romantic partner. (Mr. Zhao is Binance’s majority shareholder but doesn’t have a formal role at the company.)

“Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares,” Ms. He wrote.

With the industry reeling, Ms. He and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, told Binance employees to “stay disciplined,” according to a message reviewed by The Times.

"Do not speculate internally or externally,” the message said. “We know this is an intense moment, and we deeply appreciate everyone working overtime to make this right.”

They also tried to address the growing unease in the crypto world. Speaking in Mandarin in a video posted to X on Friday, Ms. He said that the rise of artificial intelligence had turned hacking into “a threat to the entire industry.”

“Of course, there are many things that we have done wrong,” she said. “We should have invested in security much earlier and more extensively, and established more rigorous standards.”

Word of Binance’s hack even reached Mr. Trump, who was asked about it by a reporter on Friday. “People never see the money anymore,” he said. “I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous. But they say they have it pretty much under control. We’ll see.”

Among the companies that rushed to Binance’s aid was the Trump family firm, World Liberty, the issuer of a coin known as USD1.

Zach Witkoff, the company’s chief executive and the son of one of Mr. Trump’s top advisers, announced on X that World Liberty had frozen $27 million in USD1 that was “associated with the Binance hack.”

“We stand by our industry partners,” he wrote.

“Thank you!” Mr. Zhao responded, followed by three prayer hand emojis.

Michael Forsythe and Dustin Volz contributed reporting.

item.title: F.D.A. Warns of Snack Bar Linked to Toddler Choking Hazard
item.description:
The Food and Drug Administration on Friday warned parents not to buy a soft-baked snack bar after receiving reports that it had completely blocked toddlers’ airways.

The bars, sold as Tractor Wheels by Once Upon a Farm, were linked to episodes in which toddlers ages 18 to 30 months experienced what the agency called “the inability to breathe.”

The F.D.A. did not specify how many reports it had received.

“When chewed, the product reportedly forms a dry, sticky mass that standard choking interventions — including back blows and the Heimlich maneuver — may fail to dislodge,” the F.D.A. said in an advisory.

The snack bars, which are made with whole grain oats and sweetened with fruits and vegetables, are sold in stores across the United States, including Costco, Target and Walmart, according to the F.D.A.

Once Upon a Farm said it had received three consumer reports of possible choking hazards and had voluntarily recalled the bars. It was not immediately clear when the voluntarily recall began.

“As part of this process and a larger evaluation of Tractor Wheels products, we are reformulating these family favorites to ensure they adhere to the highest standards,” the company said in a statement.

The F.D.A. advised parents who have the bars to throw them away.

item.title: Judge Tosses Trump’s $10 Billion Suit Against The Wall Street Journal
item.description:
A federal judge on Saturday once again threw out President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting that linked the president and the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The president had argued that The Journal had maligned his “character and integrity” when it published an article in 2025 about a lewd birthday greeting that Mr. Trump appeared to have written to Mr. Epstein more than 20 years earlier. Mr. Trump denied writing the greeting and sued The Journal, asking for $10 billion in damages.

On Saturday, Judge Darrin P. Gayles of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted The Journal’s request that the complaint be dismissed, writing that the president “has failed” to prove that The Journal had “acted with actual malice.”

Actual malice is a legal standard that must be met by public figures in defamation proceedings. It means the defendants knew what they were publishing was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.

“In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a ‘fake,’ Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story,” Judge Gayles wrote in a 20-page decision. “But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment.”

Judge Gayles dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning the claim cannot be refiled again.

“President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants,” a spokesman for Mr. Trump’s legal team said in a statement. “The president will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.”

A spokesman for Dow Jones, which publishes The Journal, said, “We’re pleased with the court’s decision.”

The president, who has a long history of vitriol against the press, has frequently turned to litigation to go after news media for coverage he deems critical or unfair as part of a broader effort to attack journalists. In recent years, he has filed lawsuits against outlets including The New York Times, the BBC, CNN and The Des Moines Register.

The dismissal on Saturday was the second time Mr. Trump’s lawsuit related to the Journal’s reporting about Mr. Epstein has been thrown out. The same judge dismissed an earlier defamation lawsuit from Mr. Trump in April, also because he had failed to adequately show that The Journal had acted with actual malice. Mr. Trump refiled his complaint in May.

Mr. Trump originally filed the defamation lawsuit against The Journal the day after the newspaper published an article on July 17, 2025, headlined: “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was From Donald Trump.” The article described a letter that appeared to be from Mr. Trump that was included in a 2003 birthday album for Mr. Epstein and contained the words: “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret.”

The letter had a drawing of a naked woman on it with Mr. Trump’s signature below the waist, mimicking pubic hair, according to the article. The Journal also included Mr. Trump’s denial that he had written the letter or created the drawing: “This is not me. This is a fake thing,” the article quoted Mr. Trump as saying.

After the article was published, a copy of the birthday book was released to House Oversight Committee members by lawyers for Mr. Epstein’s estate. It included a letter and drawing that resembled the one described by The Journal. The 238-page book was compiled by Mr. Epstein's former girlfriend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who has been convicted of aiding his campaign of sexual abuse.

The suit also named as defendants The Journal’s parent company, News Corp; its founder, Rupert Murdoch; its chief executive, Robert Thomson; its publisher, Dow Jones; and two Journal reporters.
